To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the formal facts of the case, as well as the topic of a case, are important features for predicting the outcome of a case tried by the European court of human rights; (b) the topical content of the case is more important for predicting a violation than a non-violation; (c) the formal facts and the topical content of cases are complementary features; (d) the court's decisions are not random but are driven by a set of factors that can be identified and
the textual content of a case can predict the court’s decisions with a high accuracy and that this prediction is mostly driven by the formal facts of the case.

(1) the textual content of a case can be used as a predictive feature for the outcome of the case; (2) the textual content is not the only feature that is relevant to the outcome; (3) the most important feature is the factual content; and (4) there is an important role of the topical content.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question: can we predict judicial decisions?
the question: can we build predictive models that accurately predict the outcome of cases decided by the ECHR?
the development of a predictive model that can help judges in the European Court of human rights in their decision-making process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the textual information extracted from a case is a strong predictive factor for the outcome of the case, with the formal facts being the most important one.
the court's decisions are driven by the formal facts, the legal arguments and the topics of the case, and that these factors can be captured by the N grams and topic models we used.
the formal facts are the most important feature for this task and the topical content of the case is a strong secondary feature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the textual content is a good predictor of a court's decisions.
we are able to predict judicial decisions based on textual content alone, with a high accuracy, and that this is consistent with legal realist theory.
the court's decision can be predicted based on the facts and topics of the case, but the decision cannot be explained by the facts and topics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the textual content of cases can be used to build predictive models which can be used to assist lawyers and judges.
Natural Language Processing techniques can be effectively applied to legal data and that the predictions of our models are consistent with the theory behind legal decision-making.
we can build predictive models that are able to predict the outcome of cases with high accuracy.
